name: Greek Geometric style
making_significance: Workshops organised pots into bands of meanders and figure friezes, setting the surface logic later Greek painters built on.
leaves_out: Cypriot and Levantine contacts; the unnamed potters
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Dipylon grave markers are funerary; display with care.

name: Orientalizing style (Greek and Etruscan)
making_significance: Greek and Etruscan workshops took up Near Eastern animal friezes, palmettes and griffins carried by trade, a case of motifs travelling ahead of makers.
leaves_out: Phoenician and North Syrian makers whose work was copied; the label centres Greece
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Archaic Greek style
making_significance: Life-size stone kouroi and black-figure painting fixed Greek workshop conventions, partly learned from Egyptian proportional grids.
leaves_out: Egyptian models; enslaved and metic workshop labour; original paint on sculpture
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Getty Open Content;Wikimedia Commons

name: Classical Greek style
making_significance: Canons of proportion (Polykleitos) and red-figure painting became the model that later academies taught as the norm for all art.
defined_by: Winckelmann (1764) and later historians; ancient writers such as Pliny
leaves_out: polychromy (sculpture was painted); neighbours treated as barbarians; enslaved labour in mines and workshops
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Getty Open Content;Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Core case for how a period became a universal standard.

name: Hellenistic style
making_significance: Workshops across the successor kingdoms from Egypt to Bactria spread and localised Greek forms, producing mixed idioms such as Greco-Bactrian and Ptolemaic.
leaves_out: local Egyptian, Bactrian and Levantine makers who reshaped the forms
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Getty Open Content;Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Pompeian styles (First to Fourth)
other_names: Four Styles of Roman wall painting
making_significance: August Mau's four wall-painting styles show how one scholar's typology became the way Roman interiors are dated.
leaves_out: enslaved and freed painters; provincial variants outside Campania
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Getty Open Content;Wikimedia Commons

name: La Tene art style
other_names: Early Celtic art;Jacobsthal styles (Early, Waldalgesheim, Plastic, Sword)
date_note: approx.; later in Ireland and Britain
making_significance: Curvilinear metal ornament was shared across many unrelated Iron Age groups, a style that spread without a state.
functions: clothing and adornment;war;rule and display;ritual and belief
defined_by: Hans Hildebrand (1872, type site at Lake Neuchatel); Paul Jacobsthal (1944)
leaves_out: the word Celtic lumps many peoples; wood and textile work largely lost
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Germanic animal style (Salin Styles I and II)
date_note: approx.; Style I c.400-560, Style II c.560-700
making_significance: Salin's typology of chopped-up and interlaced animals on metalwork is still the tool for dating Migration Period finds.
leaves_out: the makers themselves (smiths, often itinerant); textile work
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana
notes: Most finds are grave goods.

name: Insular art
making_significance: Irish, Pictish and Northumbrian monastic workshops merged metalwork interlace with Mediterranean book forms in manuscripts such as Lindisfarne and Kells.
functions: record and writing;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Pictish makers; lay metalsmiths; women's textile work
free_sources: British Library digitised manuscripts (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Urnes style
making_significance: The last Viking animal style, carved on the Urnes stave church portal, carried on into Irish and Romanesque metalwork.
leaves_out: continuity into Christian Irish work (e.g. Cross of Cong)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;DigitaltMuseum Norway/Sweden (CC BY items);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Carolingian art
making_significance: Court and monastic workshops revived late antique book painting, ivory and script (Carolingian minuscule), shaping later European lettering.
leaves_out: Anglo-Saxon and Irish scribes who staffed the scriptoria
free_sources: British Library digitised manuscripts (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Romanesque
making_significance: Masons and carvers along pilgrimage routes shared round-arched vaulting and portal sculpture across Latin Europe.
defined_by: Charles de Gerville (1818), Arcisse de Caumont
leaves_out: Islamic Iberian contributions; unnamed masons
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Gothic
making_significance: Masons' lodges developed rib vaults, flying buttresses and glass walls using geometric drawing rather than calculation.
defined_by: Renaissance writers as an insult (Vasari's maniera tedesca); 19th c. historians
leaves_out: masons' marks and lodge knowledge; Islamic pointed-arch precedents
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana
notes: Pair with the Bauhutte masons' lodge row in makers file.

name: Brick Gothic
making_significance: In stone-poor Baltic lands builders translated Gothic into moulded and glazed brick, following Hanseatic trade.
leaves_out: Slavic and Baltic builders; forced labour on crusader castles
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Mudejar
making_significance: Muslim and converted artisans under Christian rule carried brick, stucco, tile and carved-ceiling (artesonado) skills into churches and palaces.
leaves_out: the legal status and later expulsion of Mudejar and Morisco artisans
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Manueline
making_significance: Portuguese court masons carved ropes, armillary spheres and sea life from the voyages into stone.
leaves_out: enslaved Africans in Lisbon; the peoples reached by the voyages
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Plateresque
making_significance: Surface ornament compared to silversmith's work spread from Salamanca to New Spain facades.
defined_by: term from 17th c. writers, 19th c. historians
leaves_out: Indigenous carvers in New Spain
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Churrigueresque
making_significance: Retable makers stacked estipite pilasters and gilded carving, a vocabulary pushed further in New Spain.
leaves_out: Indigenous and mestizo carvers and gilders in the Americas
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Italian Renaissance
making_significance: The bottega system, linear perspective and the move from guild craft to 'liberal art' reshaped the status of making.

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0);Getty Open Content;Wikimedia Commons

name: Early Netherlandish painting
making_significance: Oil-glaze technique and guild-regulated workshops in Bruges and Ghent made panel painting an export trade.

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Northern Renaissance
making_significance: Printmaking (woodcut, engraving) let artists such as Durer sell images across Europe independently of patrons.

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: School of Fontainebleau
making_significance: Italian artists at the French court developed strapwork and stucco frames that spread through ornament prints.
leaves_out: French and Flemish assistants
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Baroque
making_significance: Church and court workshops combined architecture, sculpture and painting into total environments, exported by Catholic missions worldwide.
defined_by: Heinrich Wolfflin (1888); term from barroco (irregular pearl)
leaves_out: colonial workshops that built most Baroque churches outside Europe
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Auricular style
making_significance: Dutch silversmiths (van Vianen, Lutma) raised soft, ear-like forms from single sheets of metal.
leaves_out: the journeymen chasers in the van Vianen and Lutma workshops
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Rococo
making_significance: Asymmetric rocaille ornament ran through porcelain, silver and interiors via engraved pattern books.
defined_by: critics (term from rocaille, used pejoratively c.1790s)
leaves_out: Asian lacquer and porcelain models; Meissen and Sevres workers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Palladianism
making_significance: Palladio's illustrated treatise let builders reproduce villa forms from Veneto to Virginia, often built by enslaved people.

leaves_out: enslaved builders of plantation houses in the Americas
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Neoclassicism
making_significance: Archaeological finds at Herculaneum and Pompeii were turned into pattern books and ceramics (Wedgwood) for mass markets.

leaves_out: enslaved labour behind wealth that funded it; Ottoman lands the antiquities came from
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Yale Center for British Art (public domain);Wikimedia Commons

name: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
making_significance: Its return to medieval workshop ideals fed directly into Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement.

free_sources: Yale Center for British Art (public domain);Wikimedia Commons;British Library digitised manuscripts (public-domain items)

name: Gothic Revival
making_significance: Pugin tied Gothic form to honest construction, an argument about making that the Arts and Crafts movement inherited; empire carried it worldwide.

leaves_out: colonial builders who made it in Bombay, Melbourne and elsewhere
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Yale Center for British Art (public domain);Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Egyptian Revival
making_significance: Napoleon's Description de l'Egypte turned plundered and surveyed Egyptian forms into furniture and building ornament.
leaves_out: Egyptians of the time; removed antiquities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Internet Archive (public-domain scans)

name: Chinoiserie
making_significance: European makers imitated imported Chinese lacquer, porcelain and silk, building a fantasy of China that fed back into export production.
leaves_out: Chinese export painters and potters who produced to European order
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Japonisme
making_significance: Imported woodblock prints and crafts changed European graphic design, ceramics and furniture.
leaves_out: the Japanese printers and carvers; Meiji export workshops
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Orientalism (style and discourse)
making_significance: European painters and decorators staged the Islamic world as timeless, shaping how its crafts were collected and displayed.

leaves_out: the people depicted; local artists working at the same time
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Moorish Revival
making_significance: Owen Jones's Alhambra plates turned Nasrid ornament into cast-iron, tile and synagogue architecture worldwide.
leaves_out: the Nasrid and Moroccan craftsmen whose work was reproduced
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Internet Archive (public-domain scans);Met Open Access (CC0)

making_significance: British architects in India mixed Mughal and Hindu elements onto modern building types, using Indian craftsmen under colonial rule.

free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items);Internet Archive (public-domain scans)

name: Beaux-Arts architecture
making_significance: The Paris ecole's drawing and competition system exported one method of planning to capitals worldwide.

leaves_out: local builders and craft traditions in the cities where it was imposed
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Peredvizhniki
making_significance: Russian artists left the Academy and ran travelling exhibitions to reach audiences outside the capitals.

leaves_out: non-Russian subjects of the empire
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Impressionism
making_significance: Independent group exhibitions bypassed the Salon, a new model for how makers reach buyers.
leaves_out: women members (Morisot, Cassatt) often secondary; Japanese print sources
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Heidelberg School
making_significance: Settler painters' camps near Melbourne made landscape a vehicle of colonial national identity.

free_sources: Museums Victoria Collections (PD/CC BY items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Design reform movement (Britain)
date_note: approx.; 1835-36 Select Committee on Arts and Manufactures
making_significance: Reformers (Henry Cole, Owen Jones, Richard Redgrave) set rules for 'correct' flat ornament and founded schools and a museum to train industrial designers.
leaves_out: the Indian and Islamic makers whose objects were held up as models; factory workers
free_sources: Yale Center for British Art (public domain);Internet Archive (public-domain scans);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Arts and Crafts movement
date_note: approx.; name from Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society (1887)
making_significance: It argued that the conditions of making (hand, workshop, pleasure in labour) mattered as much as the object, a claim later reworked by Mingei, Swadeshi and studio craft.
leaves_out: women embroiderers and makers credited under firm names; the Indian and Persian textiles it studied; its prices put products beyond working-class buyers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Yale Center for British Art (public domain);Cooper Hewitt Open Access (CC0 metadata; images where PD);Wikimedia Commons;Internet Archive (public-domain scans)

name: Aesthetic Movement
making_significance: Designers and retailers made domestic interiors and collecting (blue-and-white porcelain, Japanese goods) a matter of taste.

leaves_out: the Japanese and Chinese makers of the collected goods
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Yale Center for British Art (public domain);Cooper Hewitt Open Access (CC0 metadata; images where PD);Wikimedia Commons

name: Private press movement
making_significance: Presses such as Kelmscott and Doves redesigned type and hand-printing, reviving the book as a crafted object.
leaves_out: compositors and pressmen; women binders
free_sources: Internet Archive (public-domain scans);HathiTrust (public-domain scans);British Library digitised manuscripts (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Craftsman style
making_significance: Gustav Stickley's workshop and magazine sold plain oak furniture and bungalow plans by mail order.
leaves_out: the factory workers behind 'handmade' marketing
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Library of Congress (public-domain items);Cooper Hewitt Open Access (CC0 metadata; images where PD)

name: Art Nouveau
date_note: approx.; named after Siegfried Bing's Paris shop (1895)
making_significance: A whiplash-line ornament system applied at once to iron, glass, jewellery, posters and buildings, erasing the line between fine and applied art.

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Paris Musees (CC0);Cooper Hewitt Open Access (CC0 metadata; images where PD);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Jugendstil
date_note: approx.; after the Munich magazine Jugend

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);MAK Vienna Sammlung Online (open-licence items; check);DigitaltMuseum Norway/Sweden (CC BY items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Modernisme (Catalan)

free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Nieuwe Kunst
making_significance: Dutch designers adopted Javanese batik techniques and motifs brought through colonial rule.

free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0);Tropenmuseum/Wereldmuseum photos on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ecole de Nancy
making_significance: Galle, Daum and Majorelle organised glass, furniture and craft firms around a shared naturalist programme.
leaves_out: factory glassworkers behind signed pieces
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Paris Musees (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: National Romanticism (Nordic)
